items.source_locator: Committee Opinion No. 783, Recommendations and Evaluation sections: sudden-onset intermittent abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting; timely diagnostic laparoscopy when torsion is suspected.
items.source_version: ACOG Committee Opinion 783, August 2019; live ACOG clinical guidance rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Ovarian/adnexal torsion commonly presents with sudden abdominal or pelvic pain and nausea/vomiting and requires timely evaluation because torsion is a surgical diagnosis.

items.source_locator: Symptoms and diagnosis sections: abnormal vaginal bleeding and pelvic/abdominal pain are ectopic pregnancy warning symptoms; rupture can cause life-threatening internal bleeding.
items.source_version: ACOG patient clinical FAQ, last reviewed April 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A positive pregnancy test with unilateral pelvic or abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding warrants prompt evaluation for ectopic pregnancy because rupture can cause life-threatening hemorrhage.

items.source_locator: HELLP syndrome section: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count; upper-abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, or malaise can occur.
items.source_version: Current ACOG patient guidance accessed and rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The combination of hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, thrombocytopenia, and upper-abdominal symptoms is characteristic of HELLP syndrome and requires urgent obstetric evaluation.

items.source_locator: Symptoms and treatment sections: severe abdominal pain, tenderness, rigid abdomen, fever and shock can occur with perforation; immediate emergency treatment is required.
items.source_version: NIH MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia page reviewed 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Sudden severe diffuse pain with fever, tachycardia and board-like rigidity is concerning for peritonitis, including from gastrointestinal perforation, and warrants emergency evaluation.

items.source_locator: Pediatrics in Review discussion of neonatal/young-infant thermoregulation: immature thermoregulatory mechanisms and higher surface-area-to-mass ratio increase susceptibility to heat loss.
items.source_version: AAP Pediatrics in Review, 2026 volume 47 issue 3; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Young infants have immature thermoregulation and physiologic features that increase susceptibility to temperature instability; temperature must be interpreted in age and measurement context.

items.source_locator: Final guidance discusses dosage selection and optimization for oncology products and the need to use regimen- and patient-specific evidence rather than assuming one body-size metric guarantees optimal exposure.
items.source_version: FDA final guidance, August 2024; current FDA page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: When a regimen is ordered in mg/m², the nurse calculates the dose from current BSA and the prescribed mg/m², while recognizing that organ function, toxicity, maximum doses and regimen-specific adjustments remain separate clinical considerations.

items.source_locator: Definition section: elimination half-life is the time required for drug concentration in plasma or total amount in the body to decrease by 50 percent.
items.source_version: NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls chapter, live clinical reference rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Elimination half-life describes the time for the drug amount or plasma concentration to fall by about 50%; it is not synonymous with a dosing interval or complete elimination time.

items.source_locator: FDA CDER discussion of NTI drugs: small differences in dose or blood concentration may lead to serious therapeutic failures or adverse drug reactions.
items.source_version: Current FDA CDER NTI standards page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: NTI drugs have a narrow margin between concentrations associated with efficacy and those associated with toxicity or therapeutic failure, so small exposure changes can be clinically important.

items.source_locator: Pharmacokinetic dosing section: loading dose is used to attain a target concentration promptly and depends principally on volume of distribution and desired concentration.
items.source_version: NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls clinical reference rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A loading dose is an initial dose intended to achieve the target concentration promptly; maintenance dosing then replaces drug eliminated over time.

items.source_locator: Final guidance addresses how impaired renal function can alter pharmacokinetics and how renal-function information should support dosage recommendations for affected drugs.
items.source_version: FDA final guidance, March 2024; current FDA page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: For drugs substantially cleared by the kidneys, renal impairment can increase exposure; dosage or interval adjustments must follow drug-specific pharmacokinetic evidence and the patient's renal function.

items.source_locator: Tool 12 / patient education guidance: assess understanding, use patient-centered communication and teach-back, and adapt education to the patient's needs and ability to engage.
items.source_version: AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Effective patient education is individualized to the patient's ability to engage and understand; symptoms, distress, fatigue, language, motivation and health-literacy needs influence timing and method.

items.source_locator: IDEAL Discharge Planning strategy: include patient/family as full partners, discuss key areas throughout the hospital stay, educate in plain language, assess understanding, and listen to goals/preferences.
items.source_version: AHRQ patient/family engagement discharge strategy, current page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Discharge education should be an ongoing process during hospitalization, with repeated discussion, patient/family engagement and confirmation of understanding rather than a last-minute information dump.

items.source_locator: Route-selection overview: route depends on drug properties, therapeutic objectives, patient condition and feasibility; routes differ in onset, bioavailability and practical limitations.
items.source_version: NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls clinical reference rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Medication route selection is clinical and drug-specific, considering desired onset, formulation/pharmacokinetics, patient condition, route feasibility and safety rather than cost or preference alone.

items.source_locator: Recovery position recommendation: place an unresponsive person who is breathing normally and does not require CPR in a side-lying recovery position when no condition requires keeping them supine.
items.source_version: 2024 American Heart Association/American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: For an unresponsive person breathing normally without a contraindication to movement, the recovery position is side-lying to help maintain airway patency and drainage while breathing is monitored.

items.source_locator: Recordkeeping section under the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act: record administration date, manufacturer, lot number, name/address/title of administrator, VIS edition date, and date VIS provided.
items.source_version: CDC VIS instructions, page updated/reviewed May 29, 2025; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Federal VIS recordkeeping requires documentation of administration date, manufacturer, lot number, administrator identity/address/title, VIS edition date, and date the VIS was provided; site and route may be documented clinically but are not the complete federal statutory set.

items.source_locator: USPSTF recommendation table specifies preventive services by population, age/sex or pregnancy status and risk criteria, with recommendation-specific applicability for asymptomatic people.
items.source_version: Current USPSTF A/B recommendation index rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Preventive screening is recommendation-specific and population-specific; clinicians apply age/sex/pregnancy and risk criteria rather than waiting for symptoms or using one universal schedule.

items.source_locator: CPSC childproofing recommendations address furniture/TV anchoring, locked storage of medicines and household chemicals, smoke alarms and age-appropriate home safety devices.
items.source_version: Current U.S. CPSC childproofing safety guide rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Young-child injury prevention uses layered environmental controls such as anchoring furniture, securing toxic products and medicines, maintaining smoke alarms and using age-appropriate barriers and outlet protection.

items.source_locator: Therapeutic relationship discussion distinguishes countertransference as the nurse's feelings or behaviors toward a client influenced by the nurse's prior relationships or experiences.
items.source_version: Open RN Mental Health and Community Concepts via NCBI Bookshelf; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Countertransference occurs when the clinician's own prior experiences or unresolved feelings shape emotional responses to the client; recognition and professional self-awareness are needed to protect clinical judgment.

items.source_locator: Therapeutic relationship section defines transference as a client's transfer of feelings associated with significant people in the past onto the nurse or other current caregiver.
items.source_version: Open RN Mental Health and Community Concepts via NCBI Bookshelf; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Transference is the redirection of feelings or expectations from an important past relationship onto the current clinician; it is not by itself evidence of a personality disorder.

items.source_locator: Defense-mechanism table defines regression as reverting to an earlier stage or less mature behavior in response to anxiety or stress.
items.source_version: Open RN psychiatric nursing content, 2025 NCBI Bookshelf edition; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Regression is an often-unconscious return to earlier or less mature patterns of behavior under stress; it should not automatically be labeled intentional attention-seeking or malingering.

items.source_locator: Dosage/administration and warnings sections: therapy is individualized; monitor fluid/electrolyte balance and renal function, with dosage titrated to response and clinical need.
items.source_version: DailyMed FDA labeling, updated June 17, 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Furosemide dosing and monitoring are individualized; kidney function, volume status, electrolyte balance and clinical diuretic response matter. A categorical claim that one diuretic class is always effective or ineffective at a given renal level is inappropriate.

items.source_locator: Adverse reactions/warnings: spironolactone can cause gynecomastia; risk is related to dosage level and duration and is usually reversible after discontinuation.
items.source_version: DailyMed FDA labeling revised May 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Gynecomastia and breast tenderness are recognized spironolactone adverse effects and merit medication assessment; the finding alone neither proves allergy nor cancer.

items.source_locator: Warnings and precautions: discontinue allopurinol permanently at the first appearance of skin rash or other signs that may indicate hypersensitivity; serious and sometimes fatal reactions including SJS/TEN are described.
items.source_version: DailyMed allopurinol label version 103, current in 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A new rash during allopurinol therapy requires prompt action because labeling directs discontinuation at the first rash/sign of hypersensitivity and warns of severe cutaneous reactions including SJS/TEN.

items.source_locator: Clinical pharmacology/mechanism section: methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and interferes with folate-dependent processes required for purine, thymidylate and DNA synthesis.
items.source_version: DailyMed FDA labeling updated in 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Methotrexate is an antifolate antimetabolite affecting folate-dependent nucleotide and DNA synthesis; its mechanisms in inflammatory disease are more complex than simply acting like an NSAID.

items.source_locator: Sulfonamide allergy guidance: structural determinants of sulfonamide antimicrobial allergy differ from nonantimicrobial sulfonamides; broad allergic cross-reactivity is not supported, while history and specific drug/reaction remain important.
items.source_version: 2022 Drug Allergy Practice Parameter Update; current parameter page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A sulfonamide-antibiotic allergy should be characterized by culprit and reaction. It does not justify assuming universal immunologic cross-reactivity with all nonantibiotic sulfonamides, though each proposed drug must still be assessed on its own risks.

items.source_locator: Cross-reactivity section: third-generation cephalosporins have lower cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy (<1%) than first/second generation; severe non-IgE reactions require different management.
items.source_version: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines penicillin-allergy page, current guidance rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Cephalosporin use after a penicillin allergy depends on the specific prior reaction and cephalosporin. Later-generation agents have low IgE cross-reactivity, while severe delayed beta-lactam reactions warrant avoidance/specialist guidance.

items.source_locator: Warnings/precautions: aminoglycosides have neuromuscular-blocking properties and should be used cautiously in disorders characterized by muscular weakness such as myasthenia gravis.
items.source_version: Current DailyMed gentamicin injection labeling rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Gentamicin and other aminoglycosides can impair neuromuscular transmission and worsen weakness or neuromuscular blockade in myasthenia gravis, so the order requires careful risk review.

items.source_locator: Comorbid cardiovascular disease/beta-blocker guidance: cardioselective beta-blockers are preferred when a clear cardiovascular indication exists; beta-blockers are not recommended solely to prevent COPD exacerbations without such an indication.
items.source_version: GOLD 2026 Report and Pocket Guide; current release rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: COPD is not an automatic contraindication to indicated beta-blockade. Current GOLD guidance favors cardioselective agents for established cardiovascular indications and does not support beta-blockers solely to prevent COPD exacerbations.

items.source_locator: Clinical pharmacology/specific populations: digoxin is primarily excreted by the kidneys; clearance correlates with creatinine clearance, and impaired renal function requires smaller maintenance doses and longer time to steady state.
items.source_version: DailyMed digoxin labeling updated January 13, 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Digoxin is substantially eliminated by the kidneys, so renal impairment can prolong its half-life and increase exposure; maintenance dosing must account for renal function, age, body size and clinical response.

items.source_locator: Administration instructions for mixing with regular insulin: draw regular insulin into the syringe first, followed by HUMULIN N; administer immediately after mixing.
items.source_version: Current FDA/DailyMed Humulin N prescribing information rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: When regular insulin and NPH are specifically ordered to be mixed, labeling instructs drawing regular insulin first and NPH second, then administering the mixture promptly.

items.source_locator: Standard Precautions page lists hand hygiene, PPE based on exposure risk, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, sharps safety, safe injection practices, sterile instruments/devices and environmental cleaning.
items.source_version: Current CDC infection-control guidance rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Standard Precautions apply to all patient care and include hand hygiene, risk-based PPE, respiratory hygiene, injection/sharps safety, equipment reprocessing and environmental cleaning.

items.source_locator: PPE removal principles: remove and discard contaminated PPE to prevent contamination of clothing, skin or mucous membranes; gown removal turns the contaminated surface inward and avoids touching exposed surfaces.
items.source_version: Current CDC Isolation Precautions prevention guidance rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Gown doffing should minimize contact with the contaminated outer surface and turn the gown inward while keeping contamination away from skin and clothing; exact doffing sequence may vary by PPE ensemble/protocol.

items.source_locator: Transmission-Based Precautions guidance requires use of the indicated PPE in addition to Standard Precautions based on route of transmission; PPE should be donned before relevant patient/environment contact or exposure.
items.source_version: Current CDC Transmission-Based Precautions page rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The indicated PPE must be available and donned before anticipated exposure under Transmission-Based Precautions. A supply shortage should be corrected/escalated rather than bypassing required protection.

items.source_locator: USP <797> scope and purpose establish minimum standards for compounding sterile preparations to minimize harm including contamination, excessive endotoxins, variability and other quality failures.
items.source_version: Official USP <797> chapter, current compounding standard including 2025 official text; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: USP <797> establishes personnel, environmental, process and quality controls for compounded sterile preparations to reduce contamination and other compounding-related patient risks; its purpose is safety, not workflow speed.

items.source_locator: ASHP sterile compounding resources emphasize compliance with USP standards, controlled environments, trained personnel, standardized processes and medication-safety safeguards for compounded sterile preparations.
items.source_version: Current ASHP compounding practice resources rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Centralized sterile compounding uses trained personnel, controlled environments, standard procedures and verification to reduce preparation and contamination risk compared with unnecessary complex bedside compounding.

items.source_locator: DEA diversion case describes manipulation of controlled-substance dispensing/waste processes and discrepancies; such unexplained transactional patterns warrant institutional investigation rather than assumptions from paperwork alone.
items.source_version: Official DEA diversion-control enforcement material; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Repeated unexplained controlled-substance discrepancies, atypical access/administration or unusual waste patterns are recognized diversion red flags that warrant investigation; no single pattern alone proves diversion.

items.source_locator: DEA disposal/destruction guidance explains practitioner responsibilities and controlled-substance disposal pathways; healthcare-facility procedures also operate under applicable state/local requirements and institutional controls.
items.source_version: Current DEA Diversion Control drug-disposal Q&A rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Controlled-substance waste must be handled and documented under applicable federal, state/local and institutional requirements. A universal federal rule requiring the same second-nurse witness for every bedside partial dose should not be asserted without the governing policy.

items.source_locator: CANDOR Event Investigation and Analysis Guide emphasizes multidisciplinary systems analysis, contributing factors, human factors, process design and corrective actions rather than reflexive individual blame.
items.source_version: AHRQ CANDOR Toolkit current module rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Modern patient-safety investigation uses systems analysis to identify workflow, staffing, technology, communication and human-factor contributors while still addressing individual accountability when appropriate.

items.source_locator: TeamSTEPPS team/leadership tools emphasize shared plan, clear roles/responsibilities, information sharing, mutual support, briefs/huddles/debriefs and coordinated team performance.
items.source_version: Current AHRQ TeamSTEPPS 3.0 curriculum rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Effective interprofessional collaboration uses shared goals, explicit roles, open information exchange, mutual respect/support and coordinated decision-making rather than suppressing one discipline's input.

items.source_locator: TeamSTEPPS framework overview identifies four core teamwork skills: Communication, Team Leadership, Situation Monitoring, and Mutual Support, with team structure central to their use.
items.source_version: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS 3.0 current curriculum rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: TeamSTEPPS centers on four teamwork skills—communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support—used within a defined team structure to improve safety and performance.

items.source_locator: TeamSTEPPS debrief tool: a short information exchange after an event designed to improve team effectiveness by reviewing performance, identifying what went well and what should change.
items.source_version: Current AHRQ TeamSTEPPS 3.0 debrief tool rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A debrief is a structured post-event review of team performance, concerns, successes and lessons with the purpose of improving future performance; it does not replace the procedural time-out.

items.source_locator: TeamSTEPPS team-event overview describes huddles as ad hoc planning/replanning opportunities used to establish situational awareness, reinforce plans and address emerging issues.
items.source_version: Current AHRQ TeamSTEPPS 3.0 curriculum rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A huddle is a brief team replanning tool used to restore shared situational awareness, adjust the plan and identify emerging safety/resource needs; it complements rather than replaces patient-specific handoff.

items.source_locator: State-law summary and statute table show substantial variation: many jurisdictions exclude expressions of sympathy/condolence, while some extend or limit protection differently for admissions, fault or accompanying statements.
items.source_version: National Conference of State Legislatures 50-state statutory summary, current page rechecked 2026-08-15; individual state law controls.
items.finding: Medical apology protections are jurisdiction-specific and statement-specific. Expressions of sympathy may be protected where admissions of fault are not, so clinicians should follow applicable state law and institutional disclosure policy.

items.source_locator: CANDOR framework integrates event investigation, communication/disclosure, patient/family engagement, caregiver support and resolution across organizational clinical, quality, risk and leadership functions.
items.source_version: Current AHRQ CANDOR Toolkit module rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Risk management participates in a coordinated adverse-event response that includes investigation, disclosure/risk evaluation and corrective action with clinical, quality and leadership functions rather than serving only as a blame-assignment office.

items.source_locator: OPPE FAQ explains that ongoing professional practice evaluation provides information to determine whether to continue, limit or revoke privileges and whether focused professional practice evaluation is warranted.
items.source_version: Joint Commission Standards FAQ updated January 7, 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Ongoing professional practice evaluation provides current competency/performance evidence for privileging decisions and can trigger focused review; a universal one-to-two-year recredentialing interval should not be substituted for the actual OPPE requirement.

items.source_locator: Quality-improvement guidance describes using measures over time to monitor progress, make performance visible and determine whether interventions are associated with improvement; dashboards are a presentation mechanism, not a substitute for analysis.
items.source_version: AHRQ CAHPS Improvement Guide page last reviewed March 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: A quality dashboard makes defined performance measures and trends visible to the care team, supporting monitoring and feedback; it complements rather than replaces valid measurement and root-cause/improvement analysis.

items.source_locator: NHLBI anemia symptom discussion includes tiredness/weakness, pale skin and shortness of breath among manifestations related to inadequate healthy red blood cells/oxygen delivery.
items.source_version: Current NIH/NHLBI anemia health information rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Fatigue, pallor and exertional dyspnea are common manifestations of anemia, although they are nonspecific and require evaluation such as CBC and assessment of the underlying cause.

items.source_locator: Polycythemia vera section describes increased red-cell production/hyperviscosity and clinically important thrombotic complications; therapy aims in part to reduce thrombosis risk.
items.source_version: Current NCI PDQ patient treatment summary rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Polycythemia vera increases the risk of arterial and venous thrombosis through increased cell mass and disease-related hematologic abnormalities; thrombosis is a major driver of morbidity.

items.source_locator: Leukemia clinical evaluation material notes fatigue/weakness from anemia, infection, easy bruising/bleeding from marrow dysfunction and bone/joint pain as possible findings prompting hematologic evaluation.
items.source_version: Official NCI SEER Training Modules current content rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The combination of fatigue, bruising/bleeding, recurrent infection, bone pain and abnormal blood counts is concerning for leukemia because marrow disease disrupts normal hematopoiesis; diagnosis requires formal hematologic testing.

items.source_locator: Signs/symptoms section: painless swollen lymph nodes plus fever, drenching night sweats and unexplained weight loss are classic Hodgkin lymphoma findings; diagnosis requires tissue evaluation/biopsy.
items.source_version: Current NCI PDQ adult Hodgkin lymphoma summary rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy with unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss is concerning for lymphoma and warrants diagnostic evaluation, including tissue diagnosis when indicated.
